The 146-Year History Behind Manhattan’s Little Red Lighthouse
Perched beneath the George Washington Bridge, the Little Red Lighthouse is one of NYC’s most charming—and unexpected—historic landmarks.

Built in 1880 in Sandy Hook, New Jersey, the lighthouse didn’t always have its current nickname; it was originally known as the North Hook Beacon. In 1921, it was relocated to Jeffrey’s Hook, a rocky point on the Hudson River near Manhattan’s northern edge, where it guided ships along the Hudson River and warned them away from the rocky shoreline.

It wasn’t until 1942 that the lighthouse became the star of Hildegarde H. Swift’s beloved 1942 children’s book, The Little Red Lighthouse and the Great Gray Bridge. The story introduced generations of children to the tiny red beacon and its much larger neighbor, cementing its now-famous nickname.

Source / Amazon
But the little lighthouse soon found itself in danger.

After the George Washington Bridge was completed in 1931, the brilliant lights from the bridge’s 600-foot towers—which now light up nightly for the first time in 94 years—overwhelmed the lighthouse’s beacon, and it was eventually decommissioned and abandoned.

By 1951, it was slated for demolition, with its cast-iron shell set to be sold for scrap. However, Swift’s beloved book had inspired thousands of children to rally behind the little beacon. Their nationwide campaign helped save the lighthouse, which was ultimately transferred to the NYC Department of Parks & Recreation.
Today, the 40-foot lighthouse still stands beneath the towering George Washington Bridge and remains a beloved destination for cyclists, picnickers, and boaters.

While the interior is generally closed to the public, Urban Park Rangers lead a limited number of tours throughout the year that bring its history to life, giving visitors the chance to climb the winding iron staircase and see the lantern room and working lens up close.
It’s hard to imagine a more delightfully tiny piece of NYC history hiding in the shadow of one of Manhattan’s biggest bridges!

Source / Historic House Trust of New York City
Inside the “Once in a Generation” $13 Million Restoration

Now, through a $13 million investment from the City of New York, the Historic House Trust is launching an ambitious “once-in-a-generation” effort to preserve and reimagine the lighthouse as a more accessible cultural destination.

In partnership with preservation design firm Henson Architecture, the project will preserve the lighthouse’s historic character while transforming the site into a more accessible, engaging, and welcoming destination for visitors.
The restoration and enhancement project will:
Restore the historic fabric of the lighthouse
Improve accessibility for visitors with disabilities
Enhance surrounding parkland and recreational areas
Upgrade safety features to welcome more children and visitors of all ages
Expand opportunities for free public tours
Improve signage and connections from public transportation
Introduce historical and artistic interpretation to bring new stories to life
While the restoration is underway, the public can explore the Little Red Lighthouse virtually through a new 3D experience that brings the landmark’s history and architecture to life.
Giulietta Fiore, Executive Director of the Historic House Trust, stated:

[T]he Little Red Lighthouse has become a symbol of our city’s history, imagination, and resilience. It is my hope that generations to come will look upon this little lighthouse, find their own meaning in its story, and see it standing tall amid an ever-changing city.

Pexels / Ben Jackson
Know Before You Go
Location: Fort Washington Park, beneath the George Washington Bridge along the Hudson River Greenway, New York, NY
How to Get There: Take the A train to 181st Street, walk west down the hill to the pedestrian bridge, and follow the Hudson River Greenway path north
Visitor Details: Accessible to walk around year-round during regular park hours (dawn to dusk) | Interior is closed to the public except for a limited number of guided tours
Cost: Free
